cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may terminate parental rights, and reversed New York's fair-preponderance standard.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.DEC-03: A substantiation finding that is used to drive a termination petition cannot rest on a lesser quantum than the clear-and-convincing floor the Court fixed for severing the parent-child bond.
relevance.DEC-05: When the agency files a dependency petition aimed at permanency, Santosky sets the constitutional evidentiary endpoint the petition must ultimately satisfy.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered service plans imposed under threat of termination are measured against the heightened proof the Constitution requires before parental rights end.
relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement is a step on the path Santosky polices, because the State must still carry a clear-and-convincing burden before the separation becomes permanent.
relevance.OUT-01: The presumption favoring reunification follows from Santosky's premise that parents retain a fundamental liberty interest until the State meets the heightened standard.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the controlling federal standard of proof for termination of parental rights in every state and tribal-adjacent proceeding.
relevance.FAIL-01: A termination or dependency order entered on a preponderance standard is constitutionally defective and subject to reversal under Santosky.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children could be taken from him, and that presuming him unfit without such a hearing also denied equal protection.
cases.quote: as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated finding that operates as a de facto declaration of unfitness cannot substitute for the individualized fitness hearing Stanley requires.
relevance.DEC-05: Filing a dependency petition triggers the parent's right to an individualized hearing on fitness rather than adjudication by statutory presumption.
relevance.ACT-02: Services may be ordered only after the parent has had the hearing on fitness that Stanley makes a condition of state interference.
relevance.ACT-05: A protective order that functionally strips a parent of custody must be preceded by the hearing Stanley requires, absent a recognized emergency.
relevance.OUT-01: Stanley's refusal to presume unfitness supports the federal preference for returning children to parents who have not been individually adjudicated unfit.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the State cannot prove unfitness at an individualized hearing, dismissal is the constitutionally required outcome.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County, North Carolina
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require appointed counsel for indigent parents in every parental-rights termination proceeding, leaving the appointment decision to the trial court in the first instance subject to appellate review.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.ACT-02: Parents ordered into court-supervised services have no automatic federal right to appointed counsel; any such right comes from state law or a case-specific due process showing.
relevance.OUT-02: Lassiter is the federal floor for counsel in termination proceedings and explains why state statutes, not the Constitution, drive most appointment practice.
relevance.FAIL-01: A reviewing court assessing reversal for denial of counsel applies Lassiter's case-by-case due process inquiry rather than a per se rule.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The plurality opinion announcing the judgment held that Washington's broad third-party visitation statute, as applied, violated the mother's due process rights because the trial court gave no special weight to a fit parent's determination of her children's best interests.
cases.quote: there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children

relevance.INP-05: When a parent asks the system for help, the fit-parent presumption limits how far the agency may convert that request into supervision over the parent's own judgment.
relevance.DEC-06: Differential response must respect the presumption that a fit parent's choices about services and household arrangements are in the child's interest.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary service plans cannot be treated as consent to displace a fit parent's decisions, which the Constitution presumes to be in the child's best interests.
relevance.OUT-02: Termination analysis begins from the premise that fitness, not a court's own best-interest preference, governs interference with parental decisions.

cases.case_name: M. L. B. v. S. L. J.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that a State may not condition an indigent parent's appeal from a decree terminating parental rights on her ability to prepay record preparation fees.
cases.quote: Mississippi may not deny M. L. B., because of her poverty, appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence on which the trial court found her unfit to remain a parent

relevance.OUT-02: Indigency cannot be allowed to make a termination decree unreviewable; the State must furnish the record needed to appeal.
relevance.FAIL-01: M.L.B. guarantees that the appellate mechanism for reversing an erroneous termination stays open to parents who cannot pay.
relevance.FAIL-06: Withholding the case record that a parent needs to seek review is itself a constitutionally cognizable transparency failure.
relevance.PMC-05: M.L.B. is the closest constitutional analogue to a records-access right in child welfare, though it runs to the affected parent rather than the public.

cases.case_name: Smith v. Organization of Foster Families for Equality & Reform
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that whatever liberty interest foster families may possess arises from state law and contract and was adequately protected by New York's existing pre-removal procedures.
cases.quote: the procedures provided by New York State in § 392 and by New York City's SSC Procedure No. 5 are adequate to protect whatever liberty interests appellees may have

relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement creates at most a state-law-derived interest, so the procedures owed on a change of foster placement are those the State itself supplies.
relevance.ACT-04: Kinship and other substitute caregivers hold a weaker, statutorily sourced interest than natural parents, which shapes what process a placement change requires.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification may proceed over a foster family's objection because the foster relationship does not carry the constitutional weight of the natural family.
relevance.OUT-03: Guardianship and kinship permanency rest on state-created entitlements whose procedural protections come from statute, not from substantive due process.
relevance.OUT-04: Youth aging out of care hold interests defined by the state and federal programs that created the placement, not by an independent constitutional family right.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a state child protection agency to protect a child from private violence, even where the agency knew of the danger, absent a custodial relationship created by the State.
cases.quote: As a general matter, then, we conclude that a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

relevance.INP-01: A mandatory report that the agency receives and does not act on does not by itself create federal constitutional liability for the harm that follows.
relevance.INP-02: Third-party reports do not generate a constitutional duty of protection; any duty to respond comes from CAPTA-conditioned state law.
relevance.INP-09: Oversight findings of systemic non-response do not translate into a federal damages remedy, because the Constitution imposes no general protective duty.
relevance.DEC-01: Screening out a report, even wrongly, is not a due process violation under DeShaney unless the State has taken the child into its custody.
relevance.OUT-06: DeShaney is the controlling limit on constitutional claims arising from a child's death where the child remained in private custody.
relevance.FAIL-03: Failure to meet federal performance standards yields administrative consequences, not a constitutional cause of action, given DeShaney's no-duty rule.
relevance.FAIL-04: Liability for a death under agency supervision turns on whether the State's custody created the DeShaney exception, not on the agency's knowledge alone.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR safety findings document performance failures that DeShaney forecloses from being litigated as constitutional violations.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality review exists precisely because DeShaney leaves non-custodial fatalities without a federal judicial remedy.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability analysis must account for DeShaney's holding that systemic failure to protect is not, standing alone, federally actionable.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's 'reasonable efforts' requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no right enforceable by beneficiaries through § 1983 or an implied right of action.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents

relevance.INP-04: A court-ordered referral cannot be grounded in a privately enforceable federal right to reasonable efforts, which Suter holds does not exist.
relevance.INP-05: Families seeking prevention services have no federal cause of action to compel the State to provide them under Title IV-E.
relevance.INP-09: Suter channels enforcement of IV-E plan requirements to the Secretary's administrative oversight rather than to private litigation.
relevance.DEC-01: A screen-out that conflicts with the state IV-E plan is an administrative compliance matter, not a privately enforceable federal wrong.
relevance.DEC-05: The reasonable-efforts finding a court makes on a petition is a funding condition, not a right the family can sue to enforce.
relevance.DEC-06: Prevention-oriented alternative response is a state plan feature whose adequacy Suter leaves to federal administrative review.
relevance.ACT-01: The federal preference for preventive services carries no privately enforceable entitlement to any particular voluntary service.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered services implement a state plan requirement that Suter holds is not enforceable by the children it benefits.
relevance.ACT-03: Reasonable efforts to prevent foster placement are a condition of federal reimbursement, not a right the child may vindicate in federal court.
relevance.OUT-01: Efforts to reunify are owed to the federal funder under the state plan; Suter bars beneficiaries from suing to compel them.
relevance.OUT-04: Extended foster care benefits flow from Spending Clause conditions that Suter treats as administratively, not privately, enforced.
relevance.FAIL-03: Suter defines the remedy for federal compliance failure as withholding or corrective action by HHS rather than private suit.
relevance.FAIL-06: Disclosure and plan obligations imposed on states as funding conditions are enforced by the Secretary, not by beneficiaries.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR review is the enforcement mechanism that Suter's holding leaves as the operative check on IV-E plan compliance.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and funding recovery are the federal levers available precisely because Suter closed the private-enforcement route.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review panels operate as a CAPTA-conditioned oversight substitute in a field where Suter denies private enforcement.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality commissions perform the systemic review function that Suter forecloses beneficiaries from pursuing in court.
relevance.PMC-06: Accountability analysis must start from Suter's rule that IV-E conditions bind states to the federal funder, not to families.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that 'domicile' under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law, that the twins were domiciled on the reservation through their mother, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction, vacating the state adoption decree.
cases.quote: In enacting the ICWA Congress confirmed that, in child custody proceedings involving Indian children domiciled on the reservation, tribal jurisdiction was exclusive as to the States

relevance.INP-11: Holyfield fixes the jurisdictional trigger: if the Indian child is domiciled on the reservation, the state system has no jurisdiction at all.
relevance.ACT-04: Placement decisions for a reservation-domiciled Indian child belong to the tribal court, not to the state agency's kinship process.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that ICWA § 1912(f) does not bar termination where the Indian parent never had custody, and that § 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family.
cases.quote: we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's “breakup” would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights

relevance.INP-11: Adoptive Couple narrows which ICWA protections attach at intake by keying §§ 1912(d) and (f) to an existing custodial relationship.
relevance.ACT-04: ICWA's active-efforts and placement machinery does not engage where the Indian parent never had custody of the child.
relevance.OUT-02: Termination of an Indian parent's rights may proceed without § 1912(d) remedial efforts when no existing Indian family would be broken up.
relevance.OUT-03: Placement preferences operate against the backdrop of Adoptive Couple's limits, which affect who may invoke ICWA in a permanency contest.
relevance.FAIL-05: Adoptive Couple constrains ICWA-based claims of placement discrimination by tying the statute's protections to actual custodial relationships.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court rejected every challenge to ICWA, upholding it against Article I and anticommandeering attacks on the merits and dismissing the equal protection and nondelegation challenges for lack of standing.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.INP-11: Brackeen confirms that ICWA's jurisdictional and procedural commands validly bind state courts in child custody proceedings involving Indian children.
relevance.ACT-04: ICWA's placement preferences in § 1915 survived the anticommandeering challenge and remain binding on state courts making placements.
relevance.OUT-03: Guardianship and adoptive permanency for Indian children must still follow ICWA's preference hierarchy after Brackeen.
relevance.FAIL-05: Equal protection attacks on ICWA's classifications were dismissed for want of standing, so those claims remain unresolved rather than rejected on the merits.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that where an unwed father had never exercised custody or legal responsibility, due process permitted a stepparent adoption to be decided on a best-interests standard without a finding of his unfitness.
cases.quote: under the circumstances of this case appellant's substantive rights were not violated by application of a "best interests of the child" standard

relevance.ACT-04: Quilloin shows that a non-custodial biological parent's veto over a kinship or stepparent placement depends on the relationship actually exercised.
relevance.OUT-02: Termination incident to stepparent adoption may proceed on best interests where the objecting parent never had custody or responsibility.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanency through adoption by an existing caregiver is evaluated by best interests when the outside parent lacks a developed custodial relationship.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that parents retain a substantial and presumptively dominant role in committing a child for mental health treatment, but that due process requires review of the admission decision by a neutral factfinder.
cases.quote: our precedents permit the parents to retain a substantial, if not the dominant, role in the decision, absent a finding of neglect or abuse

relevance.INP-05: A guardian's request for services is presumptively entitled to deference unless the agency has an actual finding of neglect or abuse.
relevance.INP-07: Medical and psychiatric disclosures do not displace parental decision-making absent a neglect or abuse finding, though a neutral check on placement is required.
relevance.DEC-06: Alternative response should preserve the parents' dominant role in choosing treatment while supplying the neutral review Parham requires.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary service and treatment plans rest on the parental authority Parham preserves, subject to independent review of institutional admission.
relevance.ACT-06: Emergency psychiatric or medical placement of a child requires an inquiry by a neutral factfinder even when a parent has consented.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed a child labor conviction, holding that the State acting as parens patriae may restrict parental control, including choices grounded in religious conviction, to protect a child's welfare.
cases.quote: the state has a wide range of power for limiting parental freedom and authority in things affecting the child's welfare

relevance.INP-01: Prince supplies the parens patriae basis on which States may compel professionals to report suspected harm to children.
relevance.INP-02: Any person's report is received under a state protective power that Prince confirms extends into the family for the child's welfare.
relevance.INP-05: Even where a family seeks help voluntarily, the State retains independent authority to act for the child's welfare.
relevance.INP-07: Health-care disclosures engage a state protective power that Prince holds may override parental and religious objections where the child's welfare is at stake.
relevance.ACT-06: Emergency medical intervention over parental religious objection rests on the protective authority Prince recognizes.
relevance.OUT-06: Prince frames the State's authority, and its limits, in cases where a child's death or serious injury follows parental conduct.
relevance.FAIL-04: The scope of state protective power Prince describes is the baseline against which an agency's failure to act is judged.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed injunctions against Oregon's compulsory public education act, holding that it unreasonably interfered with the liberty of parents to direct the upbringing and education of their children.
cases.quote: The child is not the mere creature of the State

relevance.INP-08: School-based reporting operates within a system in which parents, not the State, hold primary authority over the child's upbringing.
relevance.DEC-06: Alternative response must be structured so that service engagement does not become state standardization of family life.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary services are offered against Pierce's premise that the direction of a child's upbringing belongs to the parents.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held it may review a constitutional ruling at the behest of an immunized official, but because the case had become moot it vacated the Ninth Circuit's holding that a warrant was required for the in-school CPS interview and left that Fourth Amendment question undecided.
cases.quote: We therefore do not reach the Fourth Amendment question in this case

relevance.INP-08: Camreta vacated the leading appellate holding on in-school child protection interviews, so no Supreme Court rule governs when school interviews require a warrant.
relevance.INP-10: Escalating a screened report to an in-school interview proceeds without settled Supreme Court guidance, because Camreta wiped the circuit holding without replacing it.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that FERPA's nondisclosure provisions create no personal rights enforceable under § 1983, and that nothing short of an unambiguously conferred right will support a § 1983 action to enforce a federal spending statute.
cases.quote: We now reject the notion that our cases permit anything short of an unambiguously conferred right to support a cause of action brought under § 1983

relevance.INP-09: Findings by federal oversight bodies do not become privately enforceable rights unless Congress used unambiguous rights-creating language.
relevance.DEC-01: CAPTA screening and recordkeeping conditions are funding directives to states rather than individual rights enforceable when a report is screened out.
relevance.OUT-04: Transition-age services funded under Spending Clause programs are enforceable only if Congress conferred the right unambiguously.
relevance.FAIL-03: Gonzaga confirms that federal compliance failures are addressed through the funding agency, not through beneficiary § 1983 suits.
relevance.FAIL-06: Gonzaga is the controlling authority that federal confidentiality and disclosure statutes generally confer no privately enforceable right.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR performance requirements are administered conditions, not rights, under the Gonzaga test.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit findings of misuse do not create individual entitlements enforceable by affected families.
relevance.PMC-03: CAPTA's citizen review panel mandate is a state plan condition, lacking the rights-creating language Gonzaga requires.
relevance.PMC-04: Federal fatality review mandates direct agency conduct without conferring individually enforceable rights.
relevance.PMC-05: A public-transparency claim under a federal child welfare statute must satisfy Gonzaga's unambiguous rights-creating test to be actionable.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability model must distinguish, as Gonzaga does, between federal conditions on funding and enforceable individual rights.

cases.case_name: Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Center, Inc.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Supremacy Clause creates no private cause of action and that Medicaid providers could not sue in equity to enforce a Spending Clause requirement whose sole remedy Congress vested in the Secretary.
cases.quote: To say that the Supremacy Clause does not confer a right of action is not to diminish the significant role that courts play in assuring the supremacy of federal law

relevance.INP-09: Oversight-driven noncompliance is remedied by the federal agency's withholding power, not by private preemption suits.
relevance.OUT-04: Extended foster care entitlements created by Spending Clause conditions are not enforceable in equity against the State under Armstrong.
relevance.FAIL-03: Armstrong confirms that the designed remedy for a state's failure to comply with federal child welfare conditions is administrative funding action.
relevance.FAIL-06: Statutory disclosure duties tied to federal funding cannot be enforced through a Supremacy Clause action.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR corrective action and penalty withholding are the enforcement mechanism Armstrong identifies as exclusive in this posture.
relevance.PMC-02: Single Audit and OIG findings feed the administrative remedy Armstrong treats as Congress's chosen enforcement route.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review panels function as oversight precisely where Armstrong forecloses judicial enforcement of plan conditions.
relevance.PMC-05: Public transparency efforts cannot be converted into a Supremacy Clause suit to compel state disclosure.
relevance.PMC-06: Accountability mapping must recognize Armstrong's rule that federalism limits, not courts, govern most child welfare funding conditions.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that a public hospital's nonconsensual drug testing of maternity patients, with results reported to police, was an unreasonable search not saved by the special needs doctrine because its immediate purpose was law enforcement.
cases.quote: given the extensive involvement of law enforcement officials at every stage of the policy, this case simply does not fit within the closely guarded category of "special needs."

relevance.INP-01: A mandatory reporting scheme that is designed and operated with law enforcement at every stage cannot claim the special needs exemption from the warrant requirement.
relevance.INP-07: Medical disclosures generated by testing undertaken for investigative rather than treatment purposes implicate the patient's Fourth Amendment rights.
relevance.ACT-06: Emergency medical intervention loses its special needs character when its immediate object is to produce evidence for prosecution.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that a social worker and police officer who coerced entry into a home and directed a strip search of a child, without a warrant, consent, or exigency, violated clearly established Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
cases.quote: Under White, appellants' claim, that "a search warrant is not required for home investigatory visits by social workers," is simply not the law

relevance.INP-02: An unverified third-party report, without corroboration or urgency, does not authorize a warrantless entry to investigate.
relevance.INP-03: A social worker who brings police to compel entry does not thereby acquire an exemption from the warrant requirement.
relevance.INP-06: An anonymous hotline tip alleging only a child's crying is too thin to supply exigency for entering the home.
relevance.INP-10: Escalating a screened report into a home investigation still requires consent, a warrant, or genuine exigency.
relevance.DEC-02: Accepting a report for investigation confers no authority to enter the family home over the parent's objection.
relevance.FAIL-02: Calabretta is the leading circuit authority that coerced warrantless entry by child protection workers is an actionable constitutional violation.
relevance.FAIL-05: The court rejected reliance on the family's religiosity and home schooling as a basis for intrusive investigation.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that officials may seize a child without prior judicial authorization only on reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury, that reasonable investigative avenues must first be pursued, and that subjecting seized children to invasive medical examinations without parental notice implicated the family's constitutional rights.
cases.quote: the police cannot seize children suspected of being abused or neglected unless reasonable avenues of investigation are first pursued

relevance.INP-03: Police acting on a child protection referral must investigate before seizing, and may not rely on an unverified assertion that a court order exists.
relevance.INP-06: A hotline-sourced allegation must be run down through available investigative steps before children are taken.
relevance.INP-07: Invasive medical examinations of seized children require judicial authorization and parental notice absent a genuine medical emergency.
relevance.INP-12: Protective custody is lawful only where investigation has been pursued and imminent danger of serious bodily injury is shown.
relevance.DEC-04: The emergency removal decision fails Fourth Amendment scrutiny where reasonable avenues of investigation were skipped.
relevance.ACT-06: Parents retain the right to make medical decisions for their children, and children the right to have those decisions made by parents rather than the state.
relevance.OUT-06: Wallis shows how unexamined claims of imminent danger can produce serious harm to children in the State's own custody.
relevance.FAIL-02: Seizing children on a nonexistent court order, without verification, is an unlawful removal under the Fourth Amendment.
relevance.FAIL-04: Harm inflicted on children after the State assumes custody falls outside DeShaney's no-duty rule and is actionable.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment for a social worker, holding that a material fact issue existed on whether there was reasonable cause to believe the child faced imminent danger of serious bodily injury justifying warrantless entry and seizure.
cases.quote: Nonetheless, imminent danger of future harm is required to show exigency

relevance.INP-06: A report of past conduct, without evidence of continuing risk, does not supply the imminent danger needed to act without a warrant.
relevance.INP-12: Protective custody requires imminent danger of future harm, not merely a substantiated allegation of past abuse.
relevance.DEC-04: Agency delay in acting on a report undercuts any later claim that removal had to occur before a warrant could be obtained.

cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed the grant of qualified immunity, holding that chronic medical neglect and unsanitary home conditions did not establish exigency and that the warrantless removal violated clearly established Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
cases.quote: we hold that it was clearly established that warrantless removal of children is permissible only in cases of exigency

relevance.INP-12: Chronic neglect conditions that pose no immediate risk of serious bodily harm do not justify taking a child into protective custody without a warrant.
relevance.DEC-04: The exigency inquiry asks whether the child would suffer serious bodily harm in the hours needed to obtain judicial authorization.
relevance.ACT-03: Foster placement entered without exigency or judicial authorization is constitutionally infirm from its inception.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the record shows no imminent danger, the constitutional predicate for the case fails and dismissal is appropriate.
relevance.OUT-06: Rogers distinguishes chronic health problems from the imminent serious injury that would justify emergency state action.
relevance.FAIL-01: A removal order resting on conditions that never amounted to exigency is subject to reversal and § 1983 liability.
relevance.FAIL-02: Rogers holds warrantless removal absent exigency to be an unlawful removal for which qualified immunity is unavailable.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that removing a child from school for an examination on an emergency basis is unconstitutional where officials had reasonable time to seek judicial authorization consistent with the child's safety, though the defendants there received qualified immunity because the right was not clearly established in 1990.
cases.quote: it is unconstitutional for state officials to effect a child's removal on an "emergency" basis where there is reasonable time safely to obtain judicial authorization consistent with the child's safety

relevance.INP-04: Where time permits, an ex parte judicial order, not a unilateral agency decision, is the constitutionally required route to custody.
relevance.INP-12: Emergency protective custody is available only when the danger is such that judicial authorization cannot safely be obtained first.
relevance.DEC-04: The emergency removal decision turns on the availability of time to seek a court order, not on the seriousness of the allegation alone.
relevance.ACT-03: Placement following a removal that could have been judicially authorized is constitutionally defective at the outset.
relevance.FAIL-02: Tenenbaum is the Second Circuit's controlling statement that avoidable warrantless removals are unlawful.

cases.case_name: Croft v. Westmoreland County Children and Youth Services
cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment for the agency, holding that a caseworker who forced a father from the home on the basis of an uncorroborated anonymous tip, while holding no opinion that abuse had occurred, lacked objectively reasonable grounds and committed an arbitrary abuse of government power.
cases.quote: Even considered together, minor inconsistencies which provide no affirmative evidence of sexual abuse cannot alone establish the objectively reasonable grounds necessary to remove a family member from the family unit

relevance.INP-02: A third-party allegation that interviews fail to corroborate does not supply grounds to break up the household.
relevance.INP-06: An anonymous tip, uncorroborated after investigation, cannot justify coercive intervention in the family.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation to coercive action requires affirmative evidence, not merely unresolved inconsistencies in family statements.
relevance.DEC-01: Croft illustrates the evidentiary floor below which a report should be closed rather than acted on coercively.
relevance.DEC-02: Accepting a report for investigation does not license intervention once the investigation yields no affirmative evidence.
relevance.DEC-03: A caseworker who holds no opinion that abuse occurred has no objectively reasonable basis for a founded finding or for acting on one.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the investigation produces no affirmative evidence, the constitutional predicate for continued intervention disappears.
relevance.FAIL-01: Croft is the model case for reversal of agency action taken without objectively reasonable grounds.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers violated the Fourth Amendment by entering a private school and seizing a student for a custodial interview without a warrant, consent, or probable cause, and violated the parents' right to familial relations, although qualified immunity shielded them from damages.
cases.quote: although child welfare caseworkers may investigate allegations of child abuse without violating parents' constitutional right to familial relations, they may not do so arbitrarily

relevance.INP-01: A report from a mandated or institutional source does not authorize investigative steps untethered from reasonable suspicion.
relevance.INP-08: Interviewing a child at a private school without notifying or obtaining the consent of the parents violates both Fourth Amendment and familial-relations rights.
relevance.INP-10: Escalating a screened report into a custodial child interview requires individualized evidence, not agency convenience.
relevance.DEC-02: The decision to investigate must be executed by means reasonably related in scope to the circumstances that justified it.
relevance.DEC-03: Targeting parents as abusers without evidence giving rise to reasonable suspicion is itself a constitutional violation.
relevance.DEC-06: Non-court-involved investigative contact still must avoid arbitrary interference with the family relationship.
relevance.ACT-01: Pressure toward voluntary services backed by threats to remove children can constitute arbitrary interference with familial relations.
relevance.OUT-05: Where no evidence of abuse exists, continued agency involvement is arbitrary and the case should close.
relevance.FAIL-05: Doe v. Heck arose from an investigation triggered by a religious school's disciplinary practice and cabins investigation of families on that basis.

cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that the Fourth Amendment governs social workers' civil investigations, that the government may not seize a child from his parents absent a court order, parental consent, or exigent circumstances, and that removing a child from public school for a central-location interview requires a court order or a reasonable belief of abuse.
cases.quote: it is well established in this circuit that the Fourth Amendment regulates social workers' civil investigations

relevance.INP-03: Joint law enforcement and agency entries into a home are measured by ordinary Fourth Amendment rules on consent and exigency.
relevance.INP-04: A properly issued emergency custody order satisfies the warrant requirement for taking a child into custody.
relevance.INP-08: Removing a child from a public school for an off-site interview requires a court order or a reasonable belief that the child has been abused.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation to in-home or in-school investigative action triggers the full Fourth Amendment analysis in the Fifth Circuit.
relevance.DEC-02: Acceptance of a report for investigation does not relax the consent, warrant, or exigency requirements for entering the home.
relevance.DEC-04: Emergency removal requires reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of physical or sexual abuse if he remains at home.
relevance.ACT-05: A Texas Family Code § 262 emergency order functions as the judicial authorization that makes a protective seizure reasonable.
relevance.FAIL-02: Gates is the Fifth Circuit's controlling statement that seizure of a child without order, consent, or exigency is unlawful.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a valid ex parte emergency custody order authorized the caseworker's entry and search of the home for the named child, but that removal of the other children that evening was not supported by exigency and was not shielded by qualified immunity.
cases.quote: Gates was not the first case to require, at a minimum, some evidence of imminent danger prior to removal

relevance.INP-04: A judicially issued ex parte emergency custody order supplies the authorization that makes agency entry and seizure reasonable.
relevance.ACT-05: An emergency custody order covers only the child it names; siblings removed on the same visit need independent justification.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that social workers' warrantless entry and removal of a child violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments where no exigency existed and no special needs exception applied, while remanding on whether reliance on the state statute made the officials' conduct objectively reasonable.
cases.quote: We find no special need that renders the warrant requirement impracticable when social workers enter a home to remove a child, absent exigent circumstances

relevance.INP-12: Protective custody taken from the home without a warrant cannot be defended as an administrative or special needs search.
relevance.FAIL-02: Roska forecloses the special needs rationale that agencies commonly offer to justify warrantless removals.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that the Fourth Amendment governs social workers entering a home and that no social worker exception exists, but reversed the denial of qualified immunity to the caseworkers because that principle was not clearly established in the Sixth Circuit at the time, while affirming its denial to the officer.
cases.quote: the actions of social workers in entering a home are governed by the Fourth Amendment, and we have concluded that no social worker exception applies in such situations

relevance.INP-03: A caseworker accompanying officers into a home is bound by the same Fourth Amendment rules as the officers.
relevance.INP-10: Escalating an intake to a home visit in the Sixth Circuit now carries an express holding that no social worker exception to the warrant requirement exists.
relevance.DEC-02: Investigating an accepted report by entering a home requires consent, a warrant, or exigency, with no child-welfare carve-out.

cases.case_name: Health and Hospital Corporation of Marion Cty. v. Talevski
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that the Federal Nursing Home Reform Act's chemical-restraint and pre-transfer-notice provisions unambiguously confer individual rights presumptively enforceable under § 1983, and that the Act's remedial scheme was not comprehensive enough to rebut that presumption; the Court declined to disturb the Spending Clause § 1983 line running from Suter and Gonzaga.
cases.quote: our precedent sets a demanding bar: Statutory provisions must unambiguously confer individual federal rights

relevance.INP-09: Whether an oversight-identified violation of a federal child welfare condition can also be sued on privately is now decided under Talevski's two-step conferral-then-rebuttal framework, not under Gonzaga alone.
relevance.DEC-01: A CAPTA or Title IV-E screening or recordkeeping condition becomes privately enforceable only if its text unambiguously confers an individual right, which Talevski makes a demanding textual showing.
relevance.OUT-04: Extended foster care and transition-service provisions are enforceable by the youth only if they clear Talevski's unambiguous-conferral bar and Congress has not impliedly precluded § 1983.
relevance.FAIL-03: Talevski confirms that a systemwide performance duty owed to the funding agency is not privately actionable, while an individual-focused mandate may be, so compliance failures must be sorted provision by provision.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR performance measures are aggregate program standards of the kind Talevski distinguishes from the individual-rights language that supports a § 1983 claim.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and funding-recovery findings remain administrative, because the fiscal conditions they enforce do not speak in the individual rights-creating terms Talevski requires.
relevance.PMC-03: CAPTA's citizen review panel mandate directs state program structure rather than conferring rights on any identified beneficiary under the Talevski test.
relevance.PMC-04: Federal fatality review mandates are institution-directed commands that would have to be re-read under Talevski before any beneficiary enforcement claim could be made.
relevance.PMC-05: A transparency claim grounded in a federal child welfare statute must satisfy Talevski's unambiguous-conferral step and survive the implicit-preclusion rebuttal.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability model must be built on Talevski as the current controlling statement of when Spending Clause child welfare conditions are judicially enforceable by families.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A unanimous Court held that Title IV-D's requirement that a State's child support program be in 'substantial compliance' with federal law confers no individual right enforceable under § 1983, because it is a systemwide performance yardstick for the Secretary, and remanded for the lower courts to identify with particularity which specific statutory provisions, if any, create rights.
cases.quote: In order to seek redress through § 1983, however, a plaintiff must assert the violation of a federal right, not merely a violation of federal law

relevance.INP-09: Blessing holds that a systemwide compliance standard of the kind CFSR and OIG reviews measure is a yardstick for the Secretary, not a right an affected family can enforce.
relevance.FAIL-03: Blessing supplies the three-factor framework - intent to benefit the plaintiff, a right not vague and amorphous, and a binding obligation on the State - by which any claimed federal compliance right must be tested provision by provision.
relevance.PMC-01: CFSR-style aggregate performance measurement is precisely what Blessing held cannot support an individual § 1983 claim, because substantial compliance can coexist with unmet individual needs.
relevance.PMC-02: Blessing identifies reduction of the State's federal grant as the designed consequence of substantial noncompliance, which is the same lever that audit and funding-recovery findings pull.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review panel mandates must be analyzed provision by provision under Blessing rather than treated as part of a general entitlement to an adequately run program.
relevance.PMC-06: Blessing is the case that confined Suter to its facts and set the analytic method - identify the specific provision - that any accountability mapping of federal child welfare law must follow.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: In a suit by parents exonerated of child abuse who remained listed on California's Child Abuse Central Index with no procedure to contest inclusion, the Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and held that Monell's policy-or-custom requirement applies to § 1983 claims against a municipality whether the relief sought is damages or prospective.
cases.quote: Nothing in the text of §1983 suggests that the causation requirement contained in the statute should change with the form of relief sought

relevance.DEC-03: Humphries arose from a state central index that records findings which are merely 'not unfounded,' and it fixes who may be sued when a listed parent seeks a way to contest that finding.
relevance.OUT-05: Exoneration did not remove the Humphries from the index, so this case shows that closing or dismissing a case does not by itself undo the registry consequences of the earlier finding.
relevance.FAIL-06: A parent seeking prospective relief to correct or clear a maintained child abuse record must trace the failure to a municipal policy or custom, not merely to the acts of individual employees.

cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: The court reversed the dismissal, holding that inclusion on New York's Central Register of Child Abuse and Maltreatment, disseminated to prospective child care employers and coupled with a statutory burden on those employers, deprives the listed person of a protected liberty interest, and that the 'some credible evidence' expungement standard creates too high a risk of error to satisfy due process.
cases.quote: the dissemination of information from the Central Register to potential child care employers, coupled with the defamatory nature of inclusion on the list, does implicate a liberty interest

relevance.DEC-03: Valmonte is the leading circuit authority on what process is due before and after a substantiation finding is entered on a state child abuse register, and it rejects a 'some credible evidence' standard as too error-prone.
relevance.FAIL-01: Valmonte is the model for judicial invalidation of an agency registry scheme on procedural due process grounds rather than on the facts of the underlying allegation.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed a custody modification that moved a child from her mother to her father solely because the mother had remarried a Black man, holding that the anticipated effects of private racial prejudice cannot justify a race-based custody decision under the Equal Protection Clause.
cases.quote: Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect

relevance.ACT-03: A placement decision made by a court or agency may not rest on predicted community reaction to the child's or caregiver's race, however real that prejudice may be.
relevance.FAIL-05: Palmore is the one unambiguous Supreme Court holding that racial classification in the placement of a child is subject to the most exacting scrutiny and cannot be justified by private bias.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that a defendant charged with child abuse is entitled to have the confidential child-protective-services file reviewed in camera by the trial court for information material to his defense, but has no right to search the file himself or through counsel, and affirmed in part and reversed in part the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's broader disclosure order.
cases.quote: Ritchie is entitled to have the CYS file reviewed by the trial court to determine whether it contains information that probably would have changed the outcome of his trial

relevance.PMC-05: Ritchie is the Supreme Court's principal decision on access to confidential CPS records, and it makes judicial in camera review, not open disclosure, the mechanism for testing what must be released.
relevance.FAIL-06: Ritchie holds that a statutory confidentiality regime does not shield CPS files from all eyes, so a refusal to submit records for in camera judicial review is a cognizable disclosure failure.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that a person involuntarily committed to state custody retains substantive due process liberty interests in reasonably safe conditions, freedom from undue bodily restraint, and such minimally adequate training as is reasonable to secure those interests, and that a qualified professional's judgment on how to meet them is presumptively valid; it vacated and remanded for application of that standard.
cases.quote: The State also has the unquestioned duty to provide reasonable safety for all residents and personnel within the institution

relevance.ACT-03: Once the State places a child in its own custody, Youngberg supplies the affirmative duty of reasonably safe conditions that DeShaney's no-duty rule expressly leaves intact.
relevance.ACT-06: Decisions about restraint, medication, and treatment of a child in state custody are judged by the professional-judgment standard rather than by a court's own preference.
relevance.FAIL-04: Youngberg is the affirmative half of the analysis when a child is harmed under agency supervision: state custody creates the duty that DeShaney says private custody does not.
relevance.OUT-06: A fatality or serious injury occurring while the child is in state custody is measured against Youngberg's duty of reasonable safety and its substantial-departure-from-professional-judgment liability test.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that where an unwed father had never had a significant custodial, personal, or financial relationship with his child, New York's putative father registry adequately protected his opportunity to form one and due process did not entitle him to actual notice of the child's adoption.
cases.quote: The significance of the biological connection is that it offers the natural father an opportunity that no other male possesses to develop a relationship with his offspring

relevance.DEC-05: Lehr is the case that reconciles Stanley and Quilloin: what notice a putative father is owed when a proceeding affecting the parent-child tie is opened depends on the relationship he has actually developed, not on biology alone.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanency achieved through adoption by the child's existing household may be finalized without notice to a biological parent who never grasped the opportunity to develop a relationship, provided the State offers a workable registry mechanism.

cases.case_name: Moore v. City of East Cleveland
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The opinion announcing the judgment reversed a grandmother's criminal conviction under a housing ordinance that barred her from living with two grandsons who were cousins, holding that substantive due process protects family living arrangements extending beyond the nuclear family.
cases.quote: The tradition of uncles, aunts, cousins, and especially grandparents sharing a household along with parents and children has roots equally venerable and equally deserving of constitutional recognition

relevance.ACT-04: Moore supplies the constitutional weight of the kin relationship itself, which Smith v. OFFER's state-created-entitlement framing does not: a grandparent or other relative caregiver is not merely a creature of the placement statute.
relevance.OUT-03: Kinship permanency rests on a living arrangement that Moore holds the State may not lightly disrupt, which is a stronger footing than the statutory entitlement analysis alone.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that a periodic caseworker home visit required as a condition of continued AFDC assistance is not a Fourth Amendment search and, even if it had some characteristics of one, is not unreasonable, because the visit cannot be forced and refusal carries only the loss of benefits rather than criminal sanction.
cases.quote: We note, too, that the visitation in itself is not forced or compelled, and that the beneficiary's denial of permission is not a criminal act

relevance.INP-05: Where a family accepts public assistance or services, Wyman permits the State to condition continued aid on a caseworker home visit without a warrant, so long as refusal is met with termination of benefits rather than compulsion.
relevance.INP-12: Wyman is the leading contrary authority that agencies invoke to justify warrantless entry, and its rationale is confined to consensual, non-criminal, benefits-linked visits - which is why the removal cases in this brief distinguish it.
relevance.DEC-02: An investigating caseworker cannot read Wyman as general authority to enter a home, because Wyman rests on the absence of compulsion and the absence of a criminal-investigative purpose.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court reversed, holding that the Due Process Clause requires that a juvenile facing delinquency proceedings that may result in institutional commitment receive written notice of the specific charges sufficiently in advance of the hearing, notice of the right to counsel including appointed counsel for the indigent, the privilege against self-incrimination, and confrontation and cross-examination of sworn witnesses.
cases.quote: Under our Constitution, the condition of being a boy does not justify a kangaroo court

relevance.DEC-05: Gault is the foundational holding that opening a juvenile court proceeding that may cost a child his liberty and a parent custody triggers particularized written notice and an adversarial hearing, not informal parens patriae discretion.
relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered supervision and services follow an adjudication, and Gault establishes that the adjudication owes the child and parents counsel, confrontation, and sworn testimony rather than the judge's informal impressions.

notes: Method: every one of the 31 cases below was retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API in this session (search by case name or by official citation, then the opinion record itself) and its full opinion text was read before any quote or holding was written. No case, quote, or citation was taken from memory. Approximately 80 API requests were used.

Every quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text after normalizing only whitespace and curly quotation marks/apostrophes. Quotes are taken from the majority (or, for Troxel, the opinion announcing the judgment) and never from a syllabus, headnote, concurrence, dissent, statement of facts, or the court's description of another case.

Troxel v. Granville: the lead opinion is a four-Justice plurality by Justice O'Connor announcing the judgment. The quoted fit-parent presumption is from that opinion, not from any concurrence. Dataset consumers should note there was no majority opinion.

Camreta v. Greene is included precisely because of what it did NOT decide: the Court vacated the Ninth Circuit's holding that a warrant is required for an in-school child protection interview, so there is no Supreme Court rule on in-school CPS interviews. The circuits remain unsettled (compare Doe v. Heck (7th Cir.) on private schools and Gates (5th Cir.) on public schools).
Adoptive Couple v. Baby Girl: the CourtListener cluster (2959741) carries no reporter citation, so slip form is used per the citation rule. The case is reported at 570 U.S. 637 (2013).

Date fields are the date_filed recorded on the CourtListener cluster. Two differ from the conventional decision date because CourtListener records the later amended/rehearing-denied date: Lassiter (cluster date 1981-08-28; opinion issued June 1, 1981) and Prince (cluster date 1944-03-27; opinion issued January 31, 1944). Reporter citations and years are unaffected.

Retrieved, read, and then EXCLUDED: (1) Maryland v. Craig, 497 U.S. 836 (1990) and Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U.S. 390 (1923) - no rule statement in either majority could be quoted within the 30-word limit without dropping a stated condition or requiring ellipses; both are also peripheral to the 42 CPS decision points. (2) Southerland v. City of New York - the CourtListener text at 680 F.3d 127 (cluster 800656) is the order denying rehearing en banc with two dissents, not a panel opinion; the amended panel opinion at 681 F.3d 122 (cluster 799761) was retrieved and read, but its plain text is line-numbered such that no complete rule clause survives as a clean substring. Tenenbaum v. Williams supplies the Second Circuit rule instead.

Federal-baseline statutory reading: the node files rest on CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101-5116, incl. § 5106a(c) citizen review panels), Title IV-B/IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670-679c, 671-675), ASFA (Pub. L. 105-89), FFPSA prevention services, ICWA (25 U.S.C. §§ 1901-1963), VICAA (34 U.S.C. §§ 20301-20307), 45 C.F.R. pt. 1355 (CFSR), the Single Audit Act, FOIA/Sunshine, and the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Supreme Court has never construed CAPTA itself; there is accordingly no case law directly interpreting the CAPTA intake, screening, hotline, immunity, or citizen review panel provisions that most INP and PMC nodes rest on.

Programmatic nodes with NO on-point governing case law: PMC-01 (CFSR monitoring), PMC-02 (OIG/Single Audit), PMC-03 (CAPTA citizen review panels), PMC-04 (Protect Our Kids Act fatality commission), PMC-05 (FOIA/Sunshine as applied to state child welfare data), PMC-06 (analytic layer), FAIL-03 (federal compliance failure), FAIL-06 (disclosure failure), INP-09 (systemic audit trigger), and OUT-04 (extended foster care) are governed by no decision construing those provisions. The cases mapped to them state the outer federal limits instead: Suter v. Artist M. (IV-E 'reasonable efforts' not privately enforceable), Gonzaga University v. Doe (only unambiguously conferred rights are § 1983-enforceable), Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Center (Supremacy Clause creates no cause of action; Spending Clause conditions are enforced by the funding agency), and DeShaney (no affirmative constitutional duty to protect). Enforcement of these nodes is administrative - HHS corrective action plans, penalty withholding, OIG audit - not judicial.

There is no national Fourth Amendment rule for CPS home entry, child seizure, or child interviews; the standard is circuit law. This brief includes the circuit decisions it retrieved and read from the 2d, 3d, 5th, 6th, 7th, 9th, and 10th Circuits. Users in a given state must apply their own circuit: Andrews (6th Cir. 2012) expressly held no social worker exception exists but granted qualified immunity because that was not yet clearly established there, illustrating that the clearly-established overlay varies by circuit and by date.
All entries are published opinions of the U.S. Supreme Court or of the federal courts of appeals. No unpublished or memorandum decision was used.

The pre-existing key_cases entries in data/chains/cps/federal_baseline/*_federal_*_nodes.json were keyword-matched noise with synthetic citations. Their titles were treated only as candidate names; none survived retrieval and on-point review, and none is carried forward here.
No files in the repository were modified.

GAP-CLOSING PASS (2026-09-20): all eleven authorities the verifier named as missing were searched for on CourtListener in this session, retrieved as cluster and opinion records, and read in full before any entry was written. All eleven proved real, published, and on point, and all eleven were added. There is no authority on the verifier's list that could not be verified. Approximately 37 additional API requests were used in this pass; each added quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text under the same whitespace/curly-quote normalization used in the first pass.

Added Health and Hospital Corp. of Marion Cty. v. Talevski, 599 U.S. 166 (2023) (cluster 9404968) for INP-09, DEC-01, OUT-04, FAIL-03, PMC-01, PMC-02, PMC-03, PMC-04, PMC-05, PMC-06: it is the Supreme Court's current and controlling statement of when a Spending Clause statute creates § 1983-enforceable rights, decided twenty-one years after Gonzaga, and it supplies the two-step framework (unambiguous conferral, then rebuttal by express bar or by a comprehensive incompatible enforcement scheme) that these nodes must now be analyzed under. It was NOT added to FAIL-06, which had already reached the six-case cap with the two registry/records authorities (Humphries and Ritchie) that are more directly on point there; Gonzaga and Armstrong continue to carry the enforceability framing at that node and Talevski now qualifies them.

Added Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997) (cluster 118101) for INP-09, FAIL-03, PMC-01, PMC-02, PMC-03, PMC-06: it is the unanimous decision holding a Title IV-D 'substantial compliance' requirement to be a yardstick for the Secretary rather than an individual right, it sets out the three-factor structure (intent to benefit the plaintiff, a right not vague and amorphous, a binding obligation on the State) that Gonzaga refined rather than replaced, and it is the decision that confined Suter to its facts and requires provision-by-provision analysis.

Added Los Angeles County v. Humphries, 562 U.S. 29 (2010) (cluster 180037) for DEC-03, OUT-05, FAIL-06: it arose directly from California's Child Abuse Central Index and the inability of exonerated parents to clear their names, and it holds that Monell's policy-or-custom requirement governs § 1983 claims for prospective relief as well as damages, which determines who can be sued when a substantiation listing is challenged. DEC-03 and FAIL-06 previously had no registry authority at all.

Added Valmonte v. Bane, 18 F.3d 992 (2d Cir. 1994) (cluster 664891) for DEC-03, FAIL-01: it is the leading published circuit decision holding that placement on a state central register of child abusers, disseminated to prospective child-care employers and coupled with a statutory hiring impediment, deprives the listed person of a liberty interest, and that a 'some credible evidence' expungement standard carries an unacceptable risk of error. DEC-03 previously had no authority on what process is due before or after a substantiation finding.

Added Palmore v. Sidoti, 466 U.S. 429 (1984) (cluster 111160) for FAIL-05, ACT-03: it is the one unambiguous Supreme Court holding that a child placement or custody decision may not give effect to private racial bias. FAIL-05 previously mapped only ICWA and religion cases and had no authority on racial classification; ACT-03 gains the rule that a foster placement decision may not rest on predicted community reaction to race. Note that Palmore is a private custody-modification case, not an agency placement case, so it states the constitutional principle rather than applying it to CPS placement practice.

Added Pennsylvania v. Ritchie, 480 U.S. 39 (1987) (cluster 111822) for PMC-05, FAIL-06: it is the Supreme Court's principal decision on access to confidential child-protective-services files, holding that a statutory confidentiality regime does not shield CPS records from all eyes and that the trial court must review them in camera for material evidence. The quoted sentence and the holding are drawn from Parts III-B and III-C, which commanded a majority (Justice Blackmun joined Parts I, II, III-B, III-C and IV); Part III-A, on the Confrontation Clause, was a plurality and is not relied on here.

Added Youngberg v. Romeo, 457 U.S. 307 (1982) (cluster 110746) for FAIL-04, OUT-06, ACT-03, ACT-06: it establishes the substantive due process rights of persons in state custody to reasonably safe conditions, freedom from undue restraint, and minimally adequate training, judged by a professional-judgment standard. It is the affirmative half of the analysis that DeShaney's custody exception leaves open; FAIL-04 previously had only two cases and stated only the no-duty rule. Youngberg concerned an adult committed to a state institution, not a child in foster care, so it supplies the governing constitutional principle for state-custody harm rather than a foster-care-specific holding.

Added Lehr v. Robertson, 463 U.S. 248 (1983) (cluster 110999) for DEC-05, OUT-03: it completes the Stanley/Quilloin line on unwed fathers with the 'biology plus' rule and addresses what notice an adoption proceeding owes a putative father. It was not added to ACT-04 or OUT-02, both of which were already at the six-case cap; Moore was given the ACT-04 slot because it speaks to the constitutional weight of the kin relationship, which is the gap the verifier identified at that node.

Added Moore v. City of East Cleveland, 431 U.S. 494 (1977) (cluster 109670) for ACT-04, OUT-03: it extends substantive due process protection to extended-family and kinship living arrangements beyond the nuclear family, supplying the constitutional weight of the kin relationship that Smith v. OFFER's state-created-entitlement framing omits. Consumers should note that the lead opinion is a four-Justice plurality by Justice Powell announcing the judgment (Justice Stevens concurred in the judgment on different grounds); the quote is from that opinion and there was no majority opinion, the same caveat that applies to Troxel in this brief.

Added Wyman v. James, 400 U.S. 309 (1971) (cluster 108223) for INP-05, INP-12, DEC-02: it is the leading contrary Fourth Amendment authority that agency defendants invoke to justify warrantless caseworker home visits, and the circuit cases in this brief (Calabretta, Roska, Andrews) spend their pages distinguishing it. Its rationale is expressly confined to visits that are not forced or compelled and that carry no criminal sanction for refusal, which is why it does not license investigative entry. It was not added to INP-10, which was already at the six-case cap and already carries Calabretta, Andrews and Gates on the same question.

Added In re Gault, 387 U.S. 1 (1967) (cluster 107439) for DEC-05, ACT-02: it is the foundational due process decision for juvenile court proceedings (particularized written notice, counsel, confrontation, privilege against self-incrimination), and DEC-05 and ACT-02 addressed court proceedings involving children with no citation to it. Gault is a delinquency case; the Court expressly limited its holding to the adjudicatory stage of delinquency proceedings and disclaimed any necessary application to other stages of the juvenile process, so it states what process a juvenile court owes rather than resolving dependency procedure directly.

Coverage check after this pass: no node has fewer than two cases and none has more than six. Before this pass every node already had at least two cases; DEC-05 and FAIL-04 were the thinnest at exactly two and both were strengthened (DEC-05 to four with Lehr and Gault, FAIL-04 to three with Youngberg). Three nodes were already at the six-case maximum before this pass (INP-10, OUT-02, FAIL-02) and were deliberately left unchanged; the additions that would otherwise have gone to them are recorded in the notes above. The brief now contains 42 distinct cases, slightly above the 20-40 target, because closing every gap the verifier identified required all eleven named authorities.

Node-count caps forced three placement choices that a reader should know about: Talevski was kept off FAIL-06, Lehr off ACT-04 and OUT-02, and Wyman off INP-10. In each instance the node already carried six cases that speak more directly to that decision point. Nothing in those three authorities was found inapplicable to those nodes; they were simply displaced by closer authority.

Missing (for a later pass): Monell v. Department of Social Services of the City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1978) — the source of the policy-or-custom rule the brief reaches only through Humphries; it is the threshold authority for any §1983 claim against a county child welfare agency and belongs at FAIL-01, FAIL-02 and FAIL-06.

Missing (for a later pass): Paul v. Davis, 424 U.S. 693 (1976) — the 'stigma-plus' rule that Valmonte and every central-registry due process case applies; DEC-03 currently asserts a registry liberty interest without its controlling Supreme Court predicate.

Missing (for a later pass): Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976) — the three-factor procedural due process balance actually applied in Lassiter, Santosky and Valmonte; absent from DEC-03, DEC-05 and OUT-02, which all state conclusions that Mathews generates.

Missing (for a later pass): Wilder v. Virginia Hospital Assn., 493 U.S. 498 (1990) — the Spending Clause §1983 decision that Suter distinguished and that Blessing, Gonzaga and Talevski build on; the enforceability line running through INP-09, FAIL-03 and the PMC nodes is incomplete without it.

Missing (for a later pass): Michael H. v. Gerald D., 491 U.S. 110 (1989) — completes the Stanley/Quilloin/Lehr biological-father line the brief relies on at DEC-05 and OUT-03, and is the case that limits how far that line extends.

Missing (for a later pass): New Jersey v. T.L.O., 469 U.S. 325 (1985) — the Supreme Court's special-needs framework for searches of students at school; it is the doctrinal baseline for the in-school CPS interview question Camreta left open at INP-08 and INP-10, and the brief cites no Supreme Court school-search authority at all.

Missing (for a later pass): County of Sacramento v. Lewis, 523 U.S. 833 (1998) — supplies the shocks-the-conscience standard that governs substantive due process claims against caseworkers, which FAIL-02 and FAIL-04 apply implicitly without citing.

Missing (for a later pass): Olmstead v. L.C., 527 U.S. 581 (1999) — FAIL-05 expressly reaches disability bias in placements and investigations, yet the brief contains no disability-discrimination authority whatsoever.

Missing (for a later pass): Wisconsin v. Yoder, 406 U.S. 205 (1972) — the leading authority on religiously motivated parental child-rearing decisions against state compulsion; FAIL-05 and ACT-01 carry religion-based claims with no Supreme Court religion authority other than the 1944 Prince decision.

Missing (for a later pass): Meyer v. Nebraska, 262 U.S. 390 (1923) — the origin of the parental liberty interest on which Pierce, Troxel and Moore all rest; the brief excluded it only because no rule statement fit its 30-word quote limit, which is a formatting reason rather than a substantive one.

Missing (for a later pass): Nicholson v. Scoppetta, 344 F.3d 154 (2d Cir. 2003) — the leading federal challenge to removals premised solely on a caregiver's exposure to domestic violence; DEC-04 and FAIL-02 carry no authority on that recurring removal theory.

Missing (for a later pass): Turner v. Rogers, 564 U.S. 431 (2011) — the Court's later treatment of the civil right to counsel and of substitute procedural safeguards, which materially qualifies Lassiter's case-by-case rule as the brief deploys it at ACT-02 and OUT-02.
